text:
I found no study establishing the exact comparison: recency-preserving versus uniform deletion with identical deletion counts for every sequence. Closest evidence: [IeSRec](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-026-01197-1) deletes earliest interactions to preserve recent behavior and reports BERT4Rec improvements, but its reported ablations do not establish that matched-count comparison. [SETO](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.17802) randomly removes interactions, compacts survivors and left-pads; it provides relevant deletion evidence, rather than a controlled test of recency preservation. Thus, completing the matched-count experiment would strengthen attribution beyond these related results.

[BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690) adds learned positional embeddings to item embeddings and predicts an appended MASK at inference. Architectural inference: with position IDs tied to tensor slots and PAD excluded from attention, fixed-position PAD holes preserve surviving items’ original positions and index distances. Compaction preserves order but changes some positional embeddings and compresses gaps. With left-padding and a fixed terminal MASK, deleting only an oldest prefix leaves surviving positions unchanged; uniform interior deletion followed by compaction generally moves earlier survivors toward the end. Consequently, apparent recency-preservation gains can include positional effects. PAD holes also differ from MASK tokens: MASK remains an attended prediction placeholder.

A stronger experiment crosses deletion policy with representation: recency-preserving/uniform × holes/compaction, plus an unaugmented baseline. Match deletion counts per sequence, retain identical targets and masked-target supervision, fix terminal MASK placement, and read its actual position rather than nonpadding-count minus one. An optional compacted view carrying original position IDs helps isolate reindexing. Report policy effects within each representation and their interaction; improvement over baseline alone cannot distinguish recency selection, reduced context and positional perturbation.
